title: Linked Lists: Nodes That Point to Each Other
lead: A linked list is a chain of nodes. Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. There are no fixed slots — nodes live anywhere in memory and the pointers connect them.

sections.heading: The core idea
sections.body: Think of a treasure hunt: each clue tells you where the next one is. You cannot skip to clue 5 without following clues 1-4. Linked lists excel at insertion and deletion (O(1) if you have the pointer) but reading element N costs O(N).

sections.heading: When to use it
sections.body: Use a linked list when your program frequently adds or removes items from the front or middle, and rarely needs to jump to a random position. Stacks and queues are often built on linked lists for exactly this reason.

tryThis: Draw three nodes on paper. Write a value and an arrow (pointer) in each. Now 'insert' a new node between nodes 1 and 2 by redirecting arrows — notice you only change two pointers.
